content: Energy, in the context of physics, refers to the capacity to perform work through the application of forces within a system. Energy within a system can be altered by either adding or removing energy, as energy is a conserved quantity. Changes in energy within a system may also be associated with changes in the system's mass. Energy can be transformed into different states, allowing it to perform various types of physical work. It can be utilized in natural processes, mechanical systems, or to provide societal services such as heat, light, or motion. For instance, an internal combustion engine converts the chemical potential energy stored in gasoline and oxygen into heat, which is subsequently transformed into kinetic energy to propel a vehicle. Similarly, a solar cell converts solar radiation into electrical energy, which can then be used to power a light bulb or a computer. Energy transformations often involve a reversible process. For example, when energy is released in an exo-energetic form, more kinetic energy is released than was initially present. Conversely, an endo-energetic process converts kinetic energy into potential energy. An example of this is nuclear fusion, where hydrogen nuclei, under conditions of heat and pressure (often with a catalyst), are transformed into heavier isotopes. In nuclear decay, potential energy is released from the nuclei of heavy isotopes such as uranium and thorium. The rate of energy release can be significant. When these isotopes are exposed to high levels of neutrons, the transformation can be induced to release energy rapidly, as seen in nuclear power reactors or nuclear fission bombs. The reverse process, nuclear fusion, involves the transformation of lighter isotopes like hydrogen and helium into heavier isotopes, up to iron. This process typically requires heat, pressure, or a catalyst. There are various forms and classes of energy conversions, including: Thermoelectric systems (heat to electricity) Geothermal power (heat to electricity) Heat engines, such as internal combustion engines or steam engines (heat to mechanical energy) Ocean thermal power (heat to electricity) Hydroelectric dams (gravitational potential energy to electricity) Electric generators (kinetic energy or mechanical work to electricity) Fuel cells (chemical energy to electricity) Lamps (chemical energy to heat and light) Microphones (sound to electricity) Nuclear reactors (nuclear energy to heat) Nuclear power plants (nuclear energy to heat to electricity) Fossil fuel power plants (chemical energy to heat to electricity) Solar cells (light to electricity, including downconversion and upconversion) Solar thermal systems (light to heat) Wave power systems (mechanical energy to electricity) Windmills (wind energy to electricity or mechanical energy) Piezoelectric systems (strain to electricity) Acousto-electric systems (sound to electricity) Friction (kinetic energy to heat) Examples of energy conversion pathways in machines include: 1. In a coal-fired power plant: Chemical energy in coal is converted to thermal energy. Thermal energy is converted to kinetic energy in steam. Kinetic energy is converted to mechanical energy in a turbine. Mechanical energy in the turbine is converted to electrical energy, which is the final output. The last step is highly efficient, while the first and second steps are moderately efficient, and the third step is relatively inefficient. 2. In a conventional automobile: Potential energy in fuel is transformed into the kinetic energy of expanding gas through combustion. Kinetic energy of expanding gas is converted to linear piston movement. Linear piston movement is converted to rotary crankshaft movement. Rotary crankshaft movement is transmitted through the transmission assembly. Rotary movement is passed through the differential. Rotary movement from the differential drives the wheels. Rotary movement of the drive wheels is converted into the linear motion of the vehicle. Acknowledgments: The content on this page was initially contributed by Henry A. Hoff. Some of the original content was derived from Wikipedia.
